Applications, command-line tools and runtimes are written down first, one line each. A single bootstrap assembles a new Mac from them, and fixture tests hold the declarations to their word.

Assembly

_scripts/bootstrap runs these steps, in this order, on a new Mac. dot repeats the marked ones whenever the machine has to catch up with the declarations.

  1. 1
    .localrc.example.localrc 600

    Create the private file

    Copies .localrc.example to .localrc and restricts it to mode 600. It holds values for this machine, never credentials.

    Repeats with dot

  2. 2
    name, email

    Ask who is signing

    Prompts for the Git author name and email, and only when this Mac has no private Git identity yet.

    Bootstrap only

  3. 3
    *.symlink~

    Link the dotfiles

    Links every *.symlink file and directory into the home directory. An existing destination is never replaced silently: you skip it, overwrite it, or back it up.

    Repeats with dot

  4. 4
    defaults.tsvmacOS

    Apply the macOS defaults

    Writes the preferences tracked in _macos/defaults.tsv. Afterwards they change only when set-defaults is run on purpose.

    Bootstrap only

  5. 5

    Fit what the Brewfile declares

    Installs Homebrew, then reconciles every declaration in the Brewfile: the command-line tools on runner A, above, and the applications and fonts on runner B, further down. Nothing already installed is upgraded along the way.

    BrewfileRunner ARunner B

    Repeats with dot

  6. 6

    Run each topic installer

    A topic directory may carry an install.sh. The installers run in a fixed order, never prompt, and are safe to run again. The Mise topic fits runner C, the last one on this page, at the versions mise/mise.lock records.

    mise/config.tomlRunner C

    Repeats with dot

  7. dot

    Keep it current

    dot pulls the checkout, repeats the marked steps, then lists what could be upgraded. You pick the packages. Nothing is upgraded wholesale, and the final confirmation defaults to no.

Inspection

A declaration nobody checks is only a wish. The fixture suites build isolated home directories and fake every external command, so they exercise the whole setup without touching a real Mac.

GitHub Actions runs them, with the static checks, on macOS for every pull request and every push to main.

Read the suites See the latest runs

Run on every pull request and every push to main

  1. ShellCheck
  2. shfmt
  3. Zsh syntax
  4. Markdown format
  5. Secret scan
  6. Fixture suites

macOS runner

Decisions on record

Each contract in the repository has a written reason. These are the records behind them.

  1. Control software upgrades without maintaining a Homebrew distribution
  2. Read declarations as closed literal grammars
  3. Classify shells by who reads their output
  4. Each entry point resolves the checkout that contains it
  5. Validate catalogs whole before any effect
  6. Own Mise policy without changing project behavior
  7. Prepare tool context before dependent topic configuration
  8. Declare MCP servers once
  9. Deliver a secret to the project or the command that needs it, never to a shell

Not a universal installer

These are one person's dotfiles. Review the repository before applying it: bootstrap installs software, changes macOS preferences, and links configuration into your home directory.

Assembled by Danilo Martinelli

Twelve years of writing software, the last four spent recording and refining this setup. It is the environment the work happens in, not a demonstration.
